stack: Swift/SwiftUI, TypeScript (MV3), esbuild, Vitest+jsdom, Playwright, XcodeGen
notes: Rewrite of a shipping OSS extension, not a greenfield project. 24 T-tasks (22 from the design phase; T02a and T09a inserted by reviews) plus 19 BF, one of which was booked and unbooked without work — 42 tasks did work. 472 tests. MEASURED, not estimated: tokens are summed from the session and subagent transcripts (input + cache creation + output, cache reads excluded), 54.5M total; the subagent figure is a floor, 41 of 65 transcripts carried usage. Human minutes are the owner's own estimate, and deliberately so. Deriving them from transcript timestamps — the gap before each human turn, long gaps discarded — gave 554, and the owner said his estimate of 300 was if anything high. He is right and the method is wrong: a pause is not attention, so a gap where he glanced at a message and went back to something else is counted in full. Anyone measuring this field should ask the human rather than the clock. first_pass_accept_rate is +/-0.05, the session was compacted and part of the review log is reconstructed. questions_to_human_during_dev is 1 and honest — not a requirements gap but a budget decision the human raised himself. Two results that cut against the methodology's promise and are the reason to submit this. FIRST: the human's time was spent mostly on finding defects the agents could not, not on steering. Six of the defects were his, including the worst one. SECOND, and the finding proper: over half the real defects were outside the repository. The agents' own builds left 180 app bundles registered with LaunchServices, so macOS resolved the extension's identifier to a stray copy and the product broke on the owner's machine; a release tag prefix 404'd the Homebrew cask; CI lacked a toolchain the sibling workflow installed; and one 'could not establish' verdict had been reached while every neighbouring platform call was failing for an unrelated reason. No test could see any of them. Where an invariant lives outside the repo, only the build system can hold it — a lesson the methodology does not currently carry. What worked: mutation testing, six times killing a gate a green suite had hidden, once inside the very gate written to prevent that. The reviewer role paid for itself — 8 returns of ~29 reviews, two refuted findings that would have caused regressions — at roughly double the cost per task. Parallel executors corrupted each other's test runs three times until each was made to verify in its own git worktree.
